description: Aerial web blight is a disease characterized by white mycelial 'webbing' and dark red-brown lesions that can cover leaves/cotyledons, stems, and pods. Leaf and stem lesions can be water-soaked or fall through in the center, and they have a dark border, while discoloration on pods is dark and coalesces. The plant may wilt or show delayed maturity, and leaves/cotyledons can be tattered or dropped prematurely. This condition is more prevalent in southern states, and can be associated with nearby rice.
commonly_confused_with: Cercaspora leaf blight,Frogeye leaf spot,Southern blight
image1_citation: Tom Allen, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Tom Allen, Bugwood.org

description: The primary symptom of Alfalfa mosaic virus is light-yellow to dark-green leaf mottling. Infected plants may also have brown discoloration of the leaves/cotyledons and stunted growth. Newly-emerged leaves/cotyledons may be smaller than normal. Alfalfa mosaic virus has a wide host range and is transmitted by aphids.
commonly_confused_with: Downy mildew, Herbicide injury, Insect/mite injury, Iron deficiency, Manganese deficiency, Potassium deficiency, Zinc deficiency, Magnesium deficiency, Sulfur deficiency
image1_citation: Kyle Jensen, Wausau School District, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Kyle Jensen, Wausau School District, Bugwood.org

description: Anthracnose stem blight results in dark brown or black lesions on the leaves/cotyledons and stems, inside and out. Dark fruiting/reproductive bodies, acervuli, may appear with those lesions.
commonly_confused_with: Tobacco ringspot, Charcoal rot, Phytophthora root and stem rot, Pod and stem blight, Frost
image1_citation: Nancy Gregory, University of Delaware, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org

description: Bacterial blight can cause lesions on the leaves/cotyledons, cotyledons, stems, petioles, and pods. On the leaves/cotyledons and cotyledons, these lesions are small, angular, and reddish-brown in appearance with a yellow halo at the border. More advanced lesions can have necrotic tissue, or may cause leaf tattering. Stems and petioles typically exhibit larger, black lesions. Pods show reddish-brown lesions in an irregular pattern. Bacterial blight is typically one of the first foliar diseases to be observed each year and is favored by cool temperatures and humid conditions.
commonly_confused_with: Bacterial pustule, Downy mildew, Septoria brown spot, Soybean rust, Soybean vein necrosis, Target spot, Wildfire, Insect and mite injury
image1_citation: Gerald Holmes, Strawberry Center, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org

description: Bacterial pustule causes lesions and occasionally associated pustules. Lesions start as small pale-green flecks with yellow halos. As they mature, these lesions darken to brown and may coalesce. Inspecting lesions on the underside of the leaf may reveal small, dark pustules. Unlike some of the diseases bacterial pustule is confused with, leaf tattering and defoliation rarely occur.
commonly_confused_with: Bacterial blight, Septoria brown spot, Soybean rust, Soybean vein necrosis, Wildfire
image1_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Tristan Mueller, Bugwood.org

description: Bean pod mottle is strongly associated with the presence of the bean leaf beetle. Symptoms include light-green and mottled leaves/cotyledons, irregularly shaped brown lesions on pods, black lesions on seeds, and reduced pod yield.
commonly_confused_with: Peanut mottle, Soybean mosaic, Tobacco streak, Nutrient deficiency, Herbicide injury, Insect and mite injury
image1_citation: Connie Strunk, South Dakota State University, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Edward Sikora, Auburn University, Bugwood.org

description: Brown stem rot shows symptoms on the stems, roots, leaves/cotyledons, and in severe cases, the pods and seeds. The stems of affected plants have internal dark brown/black discoloration and the pith may hollow out. leaves/cotyledons start with interveinal chlorosis and eventually turn brown and drop off. Notably, the veins of leaves/cotyledons remain green. Root systems may be discolored or show signs of rot. In severe cases, there will be few/small seeds, and those seeds may be discolored.
commonly_confused_with: Charcoal rot, Phytophthora root and stem rot, Red crown rot, Southern blight, Stem canker, Sudden death syndrome, White mold, Herbicide injury, Fungicide injury
image1_citation: Alison Robertson, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Craig Grau, Bugwood.org

disease: Cercospora leaf blight and purple seed stain
description: Cercospora leaf blight and purple seed stain causes lesions on the leaves/cotyledons, stems, and petioles, and discolored seed. Affected leaves/cotyledons will be reddish-purple or bronze and have a leathery texture. These leaves/cotyledons may drop, but notably the petiole remains attached to the stem. Stem and petiole lesions are brick-red and elongated. As the disease progresses, these lesions grow together. Discoloration of the seed is pink or purple, and can appear as small spots, or can cover the seed completely.
commonly_confused_with: Aerial blight, Soybean rust, Soybean vein necrosis, Herbicide injury, Sunscald
image1_citation: Gerald Holmes, Strawberry Center, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org

description: Evidence of charcoal rot can be detected in seedlings that result from infected seed, and in mature (R3+ plants) that have been infected in the current growing season. Symptoms that occur throughout the plant structures include reduced plant growth and wilting, with wilted plants often having attached leaves/cotyledons. Stems and roots become grey/silver and have dark, black pinpoints (microslerotia) that cannot be scraped away easily. Charcoal rot occurs more frequently in dry conditions.
commonly_confused_with: Anthracnose stem blight, Brown stem rot, Phymatotrichum root rot, Phytophthora root and stem rot, Pod and stem blight, Southern blight, Soybean cyst nematode, Stem canker, Sudden death syndrome, White mold, Frost damage, Drought
image1_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org

description: Downy mildew is typically widespread in a field and has a greater impact on younger leaves/cotyledons (upper canopy). One of the most characteristic symptoms of the disease is the presence of fuzzy grey mycelium on the undersides of affected leaves/cotyledons, and sometimes within affected pods. Small chlorotic spots developed into yellow or pale-green lesions, which may mature to have necrotic patches. The resulting seeds may be undersized or low quality.
commonly_confused_with: Alfalfa mosaic, Bacterial blight, Phomopsis seed decay, Powdery mildew, Septoria brown spot, Soybean rust, Soybean vein necrosis, White mold
image1_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Bruce Watt, University of Maine, Bugwood.org

description: Depending on when it occurs, drought can result in overall yellowing and wilting of the plant and poor pod fill.
image1_citation: Author: Connie Strunk, SDSU Extension
image2_citation: Author: Ellsworth Christmas, Purdue University

description: Flooding can result in overall yellowing of the plant and can increase the propensity of rot to occur in the roots and stems.
image1_citation: Author: University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension
image2_citation: Author: Amy Timmerman, University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension

description: Foliar-fertilizer injury primarily impacts the leaves, resulting in chlorotic or necrotic spots, overall yellowing, and cupping, curling, and distortion of the leaves. In more severe cases, overall plant growth may be stunted. It can be identified based on the timing of foliar-fertilizer application and by following the path of the applicator. Upper leaves will be more impacted than lower leaves.
image1_citation:
Urea Burn
Author: Bobby Golden, Mississippi State University Extension
image2_citation:
Urea Burn
Author: Bobby Golden, Mississippi State University Extension

description: Frogeye leaf spot is recognized by the presence of grey/tan lesions with dark margins at its maturity. Lesions can start as chlorotic patches. As they mature, the leaf tissue in the lesion thins and the dark border shows. As lesions continue to develop, the centers may drop out and leaves/cotyledons may be dropped prematurely. Occassionally, the stems, pods, and seeds may be impacted. Stem lesions are brownish-red and elongated. Pods can have brown, sunken lesions. Seeds may be discolored and seed coats may crack.
commonly_confused_with: Aerial blight, Phyllosticta leaf spot, Herbicide injury
image1_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Trey Price, LSU AgCenter, Bugwood.org

description: Frost damage early in the season can damage seedling hypocotyls and leave water-soaked lesions on the cotyledons. Later in the season, frost damage can result in defoliation and immature seeds at harvest.
commonly_confused_with: Charcoal rot, Fusarium root rot and wilt, Phytophthora root and stem rot, Pythium seedling blight and root rot, Rhizoctonia seedling blight and root rot, Stem canker, White mold
image1_citation: Author: Mike Stanton, MSU Extension
image2_citation: Author: Mike Stanton, MSU Extension

description: The symptoms of fungicide injury can depend on the herbicide used. General symptoms include discoloration of the leaves, often with chlorotic spots, as well as leaf curling and distortion, and scorching of the leaves.
commonly_confused_with: Brown stem rot, Red crown rot, Stem canker, Sudden death syndrome
image1_citation: Author: Tom Allen, Mississippi State Extension
image2_citation: Author: University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension

description: Fusarium root rot and wilt primarily impacts the stems and roots. These structures can be a reddish-brown or a dark brown/black, and rot may occur. leaves/cotyledons typically yellow and wilt during the day, recovering at night. Overall, plants may show reduced growth.
commonly_confused_with: Phytophthora root and stem rot, Pythium seedling blight and root rot, Rhizoctonia seedling blight and root rot, Herbicide injury, Frost damage, Insect/mite damage
image1_citation: Meaghan Anderson, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Albert Tenuta, Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs, Bugwood.org

description: Green stem disorder is a condition where the stems of the plant are still green and fleshy while the pods and seeds are matured. The leaves of impacted plants may be dropped either prematurely or later than usual, or may show no symptoms at all. The stems don't show the normal senescence and are more pliable than unaffected counterparts.
image1_citation: Author: Harbach et al. 2016
image2_citation: Author: Harbach et al. 2016

description: Growth regulator injuries can result in cupping and twisting of the leaves, as well as the formation of callouses. Leaves may also be unusually elongated and thin, resembling straps. Stems may be twisted, bent, or otherwise malformed and brittle, and may also have callouses. The roots of impacted plants are typically underdeveloped. There may also be abnormal growth points in the plants with developmentally-abnormal structures.
image1_citation: Author: Bob Hartzler, Iowa State University
image2_citation:
Dicamba damage
Author: Debalin Sarangi and Amit J. Jhala

description: Iron deficiency in soybeans can be detected by the leaves and overall size and vigor of the affected plants. The leaves can show interveinal chlorosis and necrosis, especially on the upper leaves. Additionally, the leaves may be crinkled or deformed, or smaller than usual. Plant growth may be reduced overall, and maturity, especially pod development, may be delayed.
commonly_confused_with: Alfalfa mosaic virus, Soybean dwarf, Soybean mosaic, Soybean vein necrosis, Tobacco ringspot virus, Tobacco streak, Root-knot nematode, Soybean cyst nematode, Sudden death syndrome, Thielaviopsis root rot
image1_citation: Author: Bobby Golden, Mississippi State University Extension
image2_citation: Author: Bobby Golden, Mississippi State University Extension

description: Magnesium deficiency may result in stunted growth and delayed maturity. Impacted leaves can start showing interveinal chlorosis/yellowing followed by yellowing of the veins, and eventually necrosis and early leaf drop. Stems may be thinner than typical and spindly, resulting in a more fragile plant. Leaf symptoms are typically seen in the youngest leaves (upper canopy) first.
commonly_confused_with: Alfalfa mosaic virus, Root-knot nematode, Soybean cyst nematode, Sudden death syndrome, Thielaviopsis root rot
image1_citation: Author: University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension
image2_citation: Author: A. Correndo, International Plant Nutrition Institute

description: Nitrogen deficiency causes older leaves to yellow. More severe cases can result in reduced growth, spindly stems, and small root systems with poor nodulation. This condition is more common in wet or compacted soil.
image1_citation: Author: Bobby Golden, Mississippi State University Extension
image2_citation: Author: Francisco, E., Gil C., Casarin, V., and Prochnow, L.

description: Phomopsis seed decay is caused by the same genus of fungi as stem canker and pod and stem blight, and can occur with these two diseases. The primary symptom of Phomopsis seed decay is chalky, discolored, cracked, and shriveled seeds with sclerotia. Cotyledons can show red/brown pinpoint lesions. The external stem near the soil line may have red/brown streaks of discoloration, and the internal stem may have thin, irregular black lines.
commonly_confused_with: Downy mildew, White mold
image1_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org

description: Phosphorous deficiency causes older leaves to become dull and become discolored, turning a dull bluish-green. The leaves may also start cupping and maturity may be delayed. This condition is more common in cold and wet soils.
image1_citation: Author: Luiz Antonia Zanao Junior (IPNI)
image2_citation: Author: Bobby Golden, Mississippi State University Extension

description: Early phyllosticta infection can look like leaf scorching. Lesions typically appear near the edges of the leaf. These lesions are grey or tan in color, with dark borders. As the disease matures, small black specks (pycnidia) will form in the center of the lesions. Lesions can spread to petioles, stems, and pods.
commonly_confused_with: Frogeye leaf spot, Septoria brown spot, Soybean vein necrosis, Nutrient deficiency, Herbicide injury
image1_citation: Author: D. Mueller, Crop Protection Network
image2_citation: Author: A. Sisson, Crop Protection Network

description: Phymatotrichum root rot impacts the roots, stems, and leaves/cotyledons. Infection can result in overall reduced growth and propensity for lodging, due to the brittleness and rot of the stems and roots. The roots and stems can be darkly discolored, often with a soil line on the lower stem, and plants can be easily pulled up due to the brittleness and rot of the roots. The roots may also have a 'fuzzy' texture resulting from fungal growth. leaves/cotyledons will yellow and drop suddenly, or turn a dull green or bronze color and become dry and fragile.
commonly_confused_with: Charcoal rot,  Southern blight
image1_citation: Tom Isakeit, Crop Protection Network
image2_citation: Tom Isakeit, Crop Protection Network

description: Phytophthora root and stem rot results in dark discoloration and rot of the roots and stems, as well as yellowing, wilting, and dropping of the leaves/cotyledons. The internal tissue of the stems is watersoaked. Plant death due to phytophthora can occur quickly. This disease is more common in poorly-drained soils.
commonly_confused_with: Anthracnose stem blight, Brown stem rot, Charcoal rot, Fusarium root rot and wilt, Pythium seedling blight and root rot, Rhizoctonia seedling blight and root rot, Stem canker, Sudden death syndrome, White mold, Herbicide injury, Frost damage Insect/mite injury
image1_citation: Cary Hicks, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Vinicius Garnica, Bugwood.org

description: Pod and stem blight can be recognized by the lines of dark, raised pinpoints (pycnidia) along the stems and sometimes on the pods. Dark lesions without pycnidia may occur along the stems and pods as well.
commonly_confused_with: Anthracnose stem blight, Charcoal rot
image1_citation: Alison Robertson, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org

description: Potassium deficiencies can result in smaller plants with delayed maturity and a propensity for lodging due to weaker stems. The leaves of impacted plants often show chlorosis or necrosis starting at the leaf edges or with an interveinal pattern. Leaves may also be curled or otherwise distoried. Root systems of impacted plants are typically smaller and show poor development in comparison to healthy counterparts.
commonly_confused_with: Alfalfa mosaic virus, Soybean dwarf, Soybean mosaic, Soybean vein necrosis, Tobacco ringspot virus, Tobacco streak, Root-knot nematode, Soybean cyst nematode, Sudden death syndrome, Thielaviopsis root rot
image1_citation: Author: Bobby Golden, Mississippi State University Extension
image2_citation: Author: Bobby Golden, Mississippi State University Extension

description: Fluffy white mycelial growth is the characteristic sign of powdery mildew infection. In severe cases, chlorosis and vein necrosis may occur. Infected seed may be small, shriveled, or remain green at maturity.
commonly_confused_with: Downy mildew, Soybean vein necrosis
image1_citation: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: Gerald Holmes, Strawberry Center, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, Bugwood.org

disease: Pythium seedling blight and root rot
description: Pythium seedling blight and root rot primarily impacts seedlings (VE-V4). Roots can show poor development, and both roots and stems may be rotting. Dark, watersoaked lesions can occur on the stems and cotyledons. Leaves may yellow and drop off. Infection often occurs in isolated plants or in small patches.
commonly_confused_with: Fusarium root rot and wilt, Phytophthora root and stem rot, Rhizoctonia seedling blight and root rot, Herbicide injury, Frost damage, Flooding, Insect/mite injury
image1_citation: Martin Chilvers, Bugwood.org
image2_citation: T. Mueller, Crop Protection Network

description: The most distinct symptom of red crown rot is the presence of reddish-orange fruiting/reproductive bodies (perithecia) on the lower stems and roots. Both stems and roots show rot, and both can show a grayish-brown discoloration under the perithecia. Leaves exhibit interveinal chlorosis, wilting, and may drop early. The interveinal parts of the leaves can turn brown.
commonly_confused_with: Brown stem rot, Root-knot nematode, Southern blight, Stem canker, Sudden death syndrome, Thielaviopsis root rot, Herbicide injury, Fungicide injury
image1_citation: Author: N. Kleczewski, Crop Protection Network
image2_citation: Author: S. Geisler, Crop Protection Network

disease: Rhizoctonia seedling blight and root rot
description: Rhizoctonia results in reddish-brown, sunken lesions at the base of the stem, which can cause girdling. The leaves may yellow and growth may be stunted.

image2_citation: Author: D. Malvick, Univ. of Minnesota

description: Root knot nematodes can cause wilting, stunted growth, and result in reduced yield. The most distinct symptom is the presence of galls on the roots. The leaves will typically yellow, and wilting may occur in higher temperatures or drier conditions. Fewer and smaller pods may be produced.

image2_citation: Travis Faske, University of Arkansas - Division of Agriculture, Bugwood.org

description: Septoria brown spot results in small, dark purple or brown lesions with halos on the leaves/cotyledons. These lesions typically started in the lower canopy. As the disease develops, these lesions coalesce and can result in leaf drop. In some cases, lesions may also be present on the stems, petioles, and buds.

image2_citation: Gerald Holmes, Strawberry Center, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, Bugwood.org

description: Southern blight can cause wilting and girdling of the plant, sometimes resulting in plant death. Symptoms include brown, sunken lesions on the lower stems, the presence of white mycelium and tan/brown spots (sclerotia), stem and root rot, and the yellowing of leaves.

image2_citation: Author: T. Faske, Crop Protection Network

image2_citation: Craig Grau, Bugwood.org

description: Soybean dwarf results in stunted growth, delayed maturity, and overall yellowing of the affected plants. leaves/cotyledons are commonly smaller than usual, with a thicker texture, and may be curled or puckered. This disease is spread by aphids.
commonly_confused_with: Iron deficiency, Manganese deficiency, Potassium deficiency, Zinc deficiency, Insect/mite injury

image2_citation: A. Sisson, Crop Protection Network

description: Soybean mosaic virus may result in either chlorotic or dark-green mottled and puckered leaves/cotyledons. image2_citation: Edward Sikora, Auburn University, Bugwood.org

The disease is typically sporadically distributed in the field. Soybean vein necrosis can often be distinguished from similar diseases by the distinct veinal patterns of the early symptoms.

description: Sulfur deficiency can result in overall stunted growth and delayed maturity. The leaves yellow, often in an interveinal pattern. image2_citation: Author: Patrick Jones, NC State PDIC

description: White mold can impact the leaves, stems, pods, and seeds. A defining characteristic of white mold is the cottony, white mycelium that can be found on most structures, including on the seeds. It is distinguished from similar diseases by the grayish-white stem lesions (tyically near the nodes) and the presence of dark, black sclerotia inside the stems and pods. The leaves may wilt, turn gray-ish green or brown, and often become brittle, although they typically will not be dropped from the plant. Seeds impacted by white mold may be small, shrivelled, and covered in white, cottony growth.

description: Wildfire can cause stunted growth, girdling, and lodging of the stem. Lesions on the leaves/cotyledons and stems start as dark-green, water-soaked lesions with light margins. As the disease progresses, the lesions expand along leaf veins and can become necrotic. Affected pods have dark, water-soaked lesions.
commonly_confused_with: Bacterial blight, Bacterial pustule, Target spot

description: Zinc deficiencies, like other nutrient deficiencies, can result in overall reduced plant growth and delayed maturity. Impacted leaves often show interveinal chlorosis or yellowing, as well as interveinal necrosis. Leaves may also turn a bronze-brown color or become brittle and crinkled. The leaf edges may be puckered or distorted. A characteristic symptoms of zinc deficiency is the shortening of node lengths, resulting in a rosette-like appearance of the upper plant.
